text:
Abraham is bidden to take his son, his only son, whom he loves; and of what he feels at the bidding we are told nothing. The narrator never looks within him. He does not protest; he does not bargain. A question is raised which the writer leaves unanswered, and in this place Abraham is less a character than a silence. In that silence lies the whole meaning of the episode, and in it we hear no echo of the man who pleaded for Sodom.

The three days of travel may be read as a kind of suspended sentence: outwardly nothing happens, inwardly everything. We hear of the servants, the wood, the knife, the fire; the instruments of the act are named before the act itself. Obedience and horror are kept side by side throughout, and neither is suffered to prevail over the other. Faith, as the writer conceives it here, has less the character of a feeling than of a geometry, laid out in wood and fire and iron.

Isaac is the child of the covenant, through whom the nations are to be blessed; and that promise is now turned into a test, so that, when the two are compared, the difference between them narrows. Much depends upon a single word, _hineni_, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times: to God, to Isaac, and to the angel. Each time it means something different; each time it costs him more. For Abraham, to declare himself present is to stand nearer to his loss.

What Isaac knows we are not told. He carries the wood; he asks about the lamb; he receives an answer which is no answer. Of his thoughts the narrator gives nothing, only the plain statement that they went, both of them, together; and the phrase recurs, as though repetition might serve instead of explanation. Obedience, strictly reckoned, leaves nothing over. The question of Isaac's consent is raised, and then quietly laid down.

The reader who attends to what is missing will be rewarded. Sarah has no part in the chapter, and her death is announced in the very next verse; without its being stated, we are made to feel that something in the household did not survive the mountain. The narrator turns away at the moment when a lesser storyteller would linger, and what he omits is a part of his meaning; his silence testifies where it might seem merely to be wanting. Abraham returns to the servants; of Isaac nothing is said.

It may be objected that the reticence of the chapter reflects no more than the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains; and in some sense this may be true. Yet the reticence here is deliberate, and the writer knew what he was about. In his hands restraint is a kind of accusation, for elsewhere he tells us freely what his persons feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps.

Between the God who promises and the God who demands no settlement is reached; the writer keeps both before us and will not choose. The question cannot be answered, and its unanswerableness is itself the answer. To read the chapter is to be tried by it; and the reader, like Abraham, is left upon the mountain, the knife raised and the ram not yet seen.

Genesis 22, then, is less a story of sacrifice than a story of reading, and the lesson to be drawn from it is that the most important things are those which a writer declines to say. Each gap in it makes its demand upon us; the brevity of the chapter is the reader's burden, and what is withheld is what is given: Abraham's silence, Isaac's question, Sarah's absence, the narrator's refusal.
